keep: The idea is named up front in plain words (each part's opposition is in ohms, the difference is direction: resistor along, coil up, capacitor down) with [3] on the directions and [1][2] on impedance as the AC version of resistance in ohms. The bold recap says it back.

The brief's picture is the interactive: R, +jX_L and −jX_C tip to tail ending at a bold Z, φ and cos φ read out, sliders for R, L, C and f, and the wave panel showing the coil's current and voltage a quarter cycle apart, which is the cause of the quarter turn.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW and DO and end on two mixed puzzles. The brief's mistakes are each caught by a DO screen with its own slip: the reactance without its angle (X_C = 10 Ω offered as 10 and +j10 beside −j10), sizes added (14 and 2 beside 10), the capacitor added upwards (8 + j16) and all sizes added (24), both reactances doubling with f (12 and 20), the coil's reactance halved or left alone when f doubles.

Worked numbers all computed from the shown rule: 6.0 Ω and 10.0 Ω at 50 Hz [27], 12.0 and 5.0 Ω at 100 Hz, 8 + j6 = 10∠36.87°, 8 − j4 = 8.94∠−26.57°, cancelling near 65 Hz, practice 12 + j16 = 20∠53.13° with power factor 0.6.

Builds on Dan's ground by name: v = L di/dt and i = C dv/dt from Calculus fundamentals, ω = 2πf and power factor from Trigonometry, the quarter turn from the first lesson, tip to tail from the adding lesson, polar form from lesson 5.
fix: Skipped causal step: the explanation goes from 'the coil's voltage is the current's wave a quarter cycle earlier' straight to 'its opposition points up' without saying why. Add: the arrows of a wave turn anticlockwise, so a wave a quarter cycle ahead is its current's arrow turned a quarter turn anticlockwise and stretched X_L times; the opposition is what does that turn and stretch, so it is jX_L. Likewise the capacitor's late voltage is a quarter turn back, multiplying by −j.
False absolute in practice: 'The size of Z is never simply R + X' is false when X or R is 0. Say instead that sizes at a quarter turn combine by Pythagoras, not by adding.

False claim in the analogy's breaks: 'the two triangles share their shape only for parts in series' is wrong, since any load's overall Z = R + jX shares the power triangle's angle. Say instead that they share their shape and angle, but one counts power, which grows with the current, and the other ohms, which do not.

Misconception from the brief not addressed: students see AC as a separate subject from DC (ModEL). Add the DC twin: with no coil or capacitor X is 0 and Z is just R, the DC resistance, and series parts still add, now as arrows.
Ambiguous formula: 'X_C = 1 ÷ 2πfC' in the explanation needs brackets, 1 ÷ (2πfC), as in the practice.
shape: Matches the recommended shape after these fixes: idea named up front, rule in words, one worked example computed from the rule (8 + j6 = 10∠36.87°, then 8 − j4 with the capacitor), the common misconception (adding sizes, 14 Ω) shown failing, a trade analogy (the power triangle in kW, kVAr and kVA, same shape and angle) with where it breaks, practice with steps, rules of thumb, a worked example and the mistakes, and a bold recap.
